R059-01.notes: P4 explicitly says 'None of this makes perspective arbitrary' (kills B); P2-P3 call the correction story 'incomplete' (kills A); D is a detail. C covers the exact geometry plus the convention of the single motionless eye.

R059-02.notes: P2 gives 'the familiar telling'; P3 opens with 'That telling is not false, but it is incomplete.' B is P4 content, C is P1 content, and nothing supports D.

R059-03.notes: 'were not failing to see; they were answering a different question, about importance or about what a viewer needed to know.' A is the view the author rejects. B overstates, because the author never ranks medieval work as more accurate. C has no support.

R059-04.notes: The next sentence says it: 'The illusion succeeds only when the viewer is made to see as the system requires.' A is true of the demonstration but is not why the author calls it revealing. C and D are unsupported.

R059-05.notes: The word is set against 'a particular way of conceiving the world,' so it means free of any particular point of view. A, B and D are the usual dictionary-sense traps.

R059-06.notes: The passage lists 'a single eye rather than two, an eye that does not move.' C reverses the flat/curved assumption, and that assumption is about the visual field, not the picture. B and D misread the setting of the demonstration.

R059-07.notes: This paraphrases 'Its geometry is exact... What is conventional is the decision to treat that single, motionless eye as the standard of truth.' A denies the convention, C calls the geometry conventional, and D's painters-versus-scientists claim is invented.

R059-08.notes: 'conventions, once learned, become invisible... judging it by rules that were themselves invented.' A is the view the author rejects. B is backwards. C is wrong, because the viewer is using perspective's standards, not rejecting them.

R059-09.notes: 'a precise solution to a problem of projection, and a quiet redefinition of what a picture is for.' B, C and D are extremes. A shares the word 'quiet' with the passage, but that alone does not give the answer away.

R059-10.notes: Literal detail: 'describing the picture as a window through which the viewer looks at the scene.' The other options borrow words from elsewhere in the passage (mirror, symbolic form, what a viewer needed to know).

fact_check: No inaccuracies found. Brunelleschi's Baptistery panel is usually dated c. 1413-1425, so 'around 1415' is acceptable. Manetti's account says he stood just inside the central doorway of the unfinished cathedral, drilled a peephole and had viewers look at a mirror. The panel is lost. Alberti's De pictura (1435) is within two decades and uses the open-window image. Panofsky's 'Die Perspektive als symbolische Form' was published in 1927 in the Vortraege der Bibliothek Warburg, and it does argue the one-eye, motionless-eye and flat-versus-curved points. Saying the hole was at the convergence point is a standard simplification and still accurate.
